title: Shared DNA segments (IBD)
fact_summary: A method that finds long stretches of DNA two people both inherited from a recent common ancestor. Since about 2023 it has been used on ancient genomes to find distant relatives across centuries and continents.

claims.text: A 2025 study explains that “recent methodological developments have made it possible to detect long shared autosomal haplotypes between pairs of ancient genomes”, “often termed identical-by-descent (IBD) segments”, and that the method was previously usable only on high-quality data from living people.
claims.certainty_reason: This records what the study reports, read in the open copy linked under Sources.

claims.text: The same study says the method “is particularly useful for detecting distant relatives”.
claims.certainty_reason: This records what the study reports, read in the open copy linked under Sources.

claims.text: It works on incomplete ancient genomes because missing parts are filled in statistically: “genotypes can be statistically imputed with high confidence” from incomplete data.
claims.certainty_reason: The authors' description of the method. The methods paper they cite has not been opened.

claims.text: Studies set thresholds for what counts. One counts pairs “sharing more than two genome segments of 12 cM or longer”; another speaks of “long IBD segments (>12 cM) that indicate recent genealogical connections”.

sources.locator: Results, “Early Medieval Magyars Fall within the Genetic Diversity of the Volga-Ural Region”

claims.certainty_reason: This records what the study reports, read in the open copy linked under Sources.

claims.text: Not every genome is good enough: of 370 ancient people gathered for one study, 275 “met the criteria” for this analysis.

claims.text: One study warns that the share of a population estimated in this way “is not necessarily indicative for census population sizes”.

open_questions.text: How reliable is the statistical filling-in of missing DNA for poorly preserved genomes? The methods papers have not been read yet.
A shared segment proves a common ancestor. It does not say where that ancestor lived, or which way people moved.
